title: Why this letter is written; the faith confessed — the Trinity
english: In keeping with this custom, then, we too observe it, and we hold it the finest of laws that everything done fittingly by those of old should stand — above all, what has been strengthened by apostolic undertaking — and so we write how we stand with regard to the faith. And we send it to you, who are taught of God, for your examination, lest we be thought to be moving the eternal landmarks that our fathers set (Proverbs 22:28): you who know not only how to distinguish the tested doctrines from the spurious, but who can also supply what is lacking, exactly and with strength, because of the perfect love that is in Christ as well. I shall proceed, then, to say the things that I learned thoroughly from the beginning — born and reared in the holy and catholic Church, things I received from tender nails onward as the very way to think, and heard from you, the God-inspired preachers.

I believe, then, blessed ones, just as I have believed from the beginning, in one God, the Father almighty, wholly without beginning and eternal, Maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of God the Father himself eternally and without passion, who knows no origin other than the Father and has his subsistence from nowhere else than from the Father: light from light, of one essence, true God from true God, co-eternal. And in one Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God the Father, who is himself known together with him as light and as God, who is in truth co-eternal with the Father and the Son, of one essence and of the same stock, and of the same essence and nature, and likewise also of the same godhead.

A Trinity of one essence, of equal honour, and sharing one throne, of the same nature, of the same kindred, and of the same glory, recapitulated into one godhead and gathered into one common lordship, without confusion of persons and apart from any contracting together of hypostases. For we believe in a Trinity within a Unity, and we glorify a Unity within a Trinity: a Trinity in its three hypostases, a Unity in the singleness of the godhead. For the holy Trinity is countable in its personal hypostases, while the all-holy Unity stands outside all counting.
translator_notes: Copy-text: Migne PG 87.3 (public domain), archive.org scan pg-87-3; Greek transcribed from the page-image PDF (p. 191, cols 3152B–3152D) because the scan's Greek OCR is unreliable. Migne's facing Latin was used as a check, not as copy-text.
'From tender nails' renders the Greek idiom ἐξ ἀπαλῶν ὀνύχων, 'from earliest childhood'.
The landmarks sentence alludes to Proverbs 22:28, which Migne's own footnote marks; the citation is given in the reading text.
New English translation made for Via Patrum (2026); no modern copyrighted translation was used.

title: Two natures, two natural operations
english: For the God who is the Word remains God the Word, and is not flesh — even though he took flesh endowed with a rational soul, and united it to himself in a union that is natural and according to hypostasis. And the flesh remains flesh endowed with a rational soul, not the Word — even though it is beheld as the flesh of God the Word. For this reason, after their natural and unconfused union — that is, the true union, the union according to hypostasis — the two do not possess an operation identical with one another's beyond all difference; nor do we call their operation one and only, be it essential and natural, and altogether without distinction, lest we also drive them together into one essence and one nature: that 'composite' operation which is the plaything of the children of the Acephali, brought out by them, in their own words, without shame.

Just as, then, we believe in the union of each of the two essences and natures — the essences and natures from which the union in Christ has come to be for us without confusion, and has made him the one Christ and Son, wholly God, and the same one wholly man — so too we confess the natural operation of each, lest we confuse the natures that were united without confusion; since, according to those who are skilled in such matters, natures are known from their operations, and from their operations alone. And the difference between essences is by nature always grasped from the difference between their operations. So too we decree that every utterance and every operation, whether one that is divine and heavenly, or one that is human and earthly, proceeds from the one and the same Christ and Son, and from his one composite and single hypostasis, inasmuch as he was the incarnate Word of God — he who also puts forth from himself, by nature, each of his two operations, without division and without confusion, in keeping with his own natures: in keeping with his divine nature, in which he was also of one essence with the Father, the godlike and ineffable operation; in keeping with his human nature, in which the same one remained of one essence with us human beings, the human and earthly operation, the operation that is proper and fitting to each nature. And he permits none of those who see to be scandalized, as though the one who works these things and those by nature were not himself God, and himself man.

By the very fact that the same one Christ and Son works the things belonging to each nature, he blocks up the foul outflow of Nestorius: for we do not, as Nestorius did, maintain that the ones who work these things and those are two Christs and two Sons, as we have said. And by showing that the properties of each nature remain unconfused after the union, and that each of them likewise brings forth its own operation — the natures being made known by their own natural principle, and each interpreting its own nature naturally, the nature from which the operation issued forth without division and by nature, and welled up in accordance with essence — he turns aside the confusion-loving offshoot of Eutyches.
translator_notes: Copy-text: Migne PG 87.3 (public domain), archive.org scan pg-87-3; Greek transcribed from the page-image PDF (p. 201, cols 3171B–3172D) and checked against Migne's facing Latin.

ἐνέργεια is rendered 'operation' throughout, its sense in the seventh-century controversy; Sophronius confesses 'each natural operation' (ἑκατέραν φυσικὴν ἐνέργειαν) of the two natures — the confession later vindicated at the Sixth Ecumenical Council (680–681) for wills as for operations.

The 'Acephali' ('Headless Ones') were the strict Miaphysite party; their slogan of one composite operation is what Sophronius refuses. Nestorius and Eutyches mark the two opposite errors the paragraph steers between.
New English translation made for Via Patrum (2026); no modern copyrighted translation was used.
